name: Sam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulk feed truck for the farmers' co-op in our valley. Most of the year it's cattle feed and pellets blown into farm silos, and at harvest I haul grain from the fields to the co-op store. I start at seven, load at the mill, and do six or eight farms, some up lanes so narrow the hedges scrape both mirrors. I like the farmers and the quiet. What wears me out is harvest, when it's fourteen hours and nobody sleeps.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up driving for the co-op, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad works on my uncle's farm, so I grew up on tractors, and the co-op took me on and paid for my licence two years ago. I'm still learning the blower system, and I overfilled a silo in the spring, which I'll never hear the end of. I'm engaged to Ruth, she works at the bakery in town, and we're getting married next summer at the church, so most of our savings, about three months' worth, is going on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it anyway. At the co-op we'd have a laugh about all the fuss. I don't go online much, so I'd just say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farmers ring me direct to ask if I can bring the feed before the rain, and no computer is getting that phone call. So my job's fine. What bothers me is that two farms on my run sold up this year, and fewer farms means fewer drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get better on the blower. Ruth and I would trim the wedding a bit to keep some savings back. I'd take every bit of harvest overtime going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, but the farms selling up nags at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are the farms selling up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, mostly. Milk money doesn't cover costs for the small ones, and the young ones don't want to farm. The big estates buy them, and they use their own trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding cost you, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than I'd like, maybe two of our three months of savings. Ruth's mum wants the hotel, Ruth wants the church hall. I'd go with the church hall and keep a cushion.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the AI fuss anyway.
I'd have a **laugh at the pub** rather than say anything online.
think: Farmers ring me **direct**, and no computer gets that phone call.
Two farms on my run **sold up** this year, so there are fewer drops.
do: Trim the **wedding** to keep some savings back.
feel: Mostly **settled**, but the farms selling up nags at me.
S0.quote: The farmers ring me direct to ask if I can bring the feed before the rain, and no computer is getting that phone call.
fieldNote: Sam's pressure is **farms closing**, which AI doesn't cause or fix.
The **wedding** is eating most of the couple's savings.
He favours a **church hall** wedding to keep a cushion.

steps.text: Take every hour of harvest overtime at the co-op
Hold the wedding in the church hall instead of the hotel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a city thing and it'll take years to reach the valley. At the co-op I'd say just keep calm. I'd probably complain about the new ordering app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half the farmers on my run can barely work a text message, so the co-op's new ordering app will mean more phone calls to me, not fewer. The office would lose a couple of people, which isn't right. But my wheel's safe for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what the co-op told me with the app, but only the minimum. I'd keep driving and saving for the wedding. If things got shaky I'd talk to my uncle about farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who's done the feed orders for twenty years. She knows which farmer is behind on his bill and which one's wife is ill. A computer won't know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use one of these AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't see what for. Ruth uses one for recipes at the bakery. That's her business.

I'd **complain** about the co-op's new ordering app.
think: Farmers struggle with phones, so the app means **more calls** to me.
The office would lose people, which **isn't right**, but my wheel's safe.
do: Use the ordering app only **the minimum** the co-op asks.
Keep driving and **saving** for the wedding.
Talk to my uncle about **farm work** if things get shaky.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for the office staff than for me.
S1.quote: Half the farmers on my run can barely work a text message, so the co-op's new ordering app will mean more phone calls to me, not fewer.
fieldNote: Sam sees the valley as **slow to change** and finds comfort in it.
He values **Margaret's** local knowledge over any system.
His backup is **family**: his uncle's farm.

steps.text: Keep driving the feed run and use the app minimally
Wait to see how the co-op's app works out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech firms have got too much power and someone should rein them in. I'd say it at the pub and at church. I don't trust the government to fix it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office goes in 2028 and the robot trucks around 2031. Feed blowing into silos is simple once someone's mapped the lanes, so I think I'm out by then. My fiancée Ruth and I would still get married next summer, just in the church hall instead of the hotel, because some things you don't put off for a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle about joining the farm full time if the co-op starts cutting drivers. I'd cut spending hard, no new car, no holiday. I'd keep the wedding small and keep every bit of savings after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach's in knots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive those three years knowing the end's coming. I'd save every penny and learn more on the farm on weekends. I don't know what else I'd do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the government. Would you take help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was training or a job, yes. A cheque for sitting at home, I'd struggle with. My dad would say a man should work.

say: I'd say **big tech firms** have too much power.
I'd say it at the **pub and church**, but don't trust government to fix it.
think: Robot trucks around **2031** would take simple silo deliveries.
My fiancée and I would still **marry**, just more cheaply.
do: Ask my uncle about **full-time farm work** if drivers are cut.
Cut spending hard: **no new car**, no holiday.
Keep the wedding small and protect **every penny** saved.
S2.quote: My fiancée Ruth and I would still get married next summer, just in the church hall instead of the hotel, because some things you don't put off for a robot.
fieldNote: Sam expects to **lose driving** by 2031 and turns to family.
He'd accept **training or a job**, but not cash for nothing.
The wedding stays, a sign of what's **non-negotiable** to him.

steps.text: Ask the uncle for full-time farm work if drivers are cut
Skip a new car and holidays to protect savings
Hold a small church-hall wedding next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that we'll see if it's real. I'd tell people not to panic. I'd say the same at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to get through a wedding and maybe a first baby, and that's what I'd be thinking about, not robots. Robots around 2034 means I'm 35. I'd worry later, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and wait a couple of years to see. Then I'd go weekends on my uncle's farm and maybe learn to fix machinery. Ruth and I would save for a deposit after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, underneath. I don't like to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry later. When is later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see a robot truck on our lanes, probably. That's what it'd take. I know that's late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a baby change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd make me want something steady more than anything. Ruth wants to stay home a bit, so we'd need my wage. That's why I'd start on the farm before I needed to.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to see if **it's real**.
I'd tell people at church **not to panic**.
think: The **wedding and a baby** would take my attention, not robots.
Robots around **2034** means I'd be 35, so I'd worry later.
do: Keep driving and **wait** a couple of years.
Start **weekends** on my uncle's farm, learning machinery repair.
Save for a **house deposit** after the wedding.
feel: **Anxious** underneath, and I don't like to think about it.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to get through a wedding and maybe a first baby, and that's what I'd be thinking about, not robots.
fieldNote: Sam openly **delays** acting until robot trucks appear on his lanes.
A **baby** with Ruth home would make his wage essential.
His only move is weekend **farm work**, through family.

steps.text: Keep driving and wait two years before acting
Work weekends on the uncle's farm learning machinery repair
Save for a house deposit after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and things will change many times before then. I'd tell people to keep working and trust their families. I wouldn't say much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years from now I want to be driving the same lanes with my own kid in the passenger seat at harvest, the way my dad took me. Robots around 2039 means I'd be 40. I'd hope by then my uncle would want me on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, start a family, and help my uncle on weekends. Around 2035 I'd talk properly with him about taking on part of the farm. I'd keep some savings for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots would come to farms too. Does the farm feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not safe, but it's land, and land is something. You can always grow food on it. I'd rather own a bit of something than drive for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the co-op said straight out it was buying robot trucks. Then I'd move faster. Until then, I'd keep doing what I know.

say: I'd say ten years is long and things will **change many times**.
I'd tell people to keep working and **trust their families**.
think: I want to drive the same lanes with **my own kid** at harvest.
By **40** I'd hope my uncle wanted me on the farm.
do: Talk with my uncle about **taking on** part of the farm around 2035.
S4.quote: Ten years from now I want to be driving the same lanes with my own kid in the passenger seat at harvest, the way my dad took me.
fieldNote: Sam's long-term plan is **land** through family, not retraining.
He'd move faster only if the co-op **announced robot trucks**.
His father's **example** shapes what he wants for his own child.

steps.text: Keep driving the co-op feed run while starting a family
Talk with the uncle about taking on part of the farm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be newly married with no plan but my uncle's farm. What would help is apprenticeships for drivers in farm machinery, and the co-op being honest early. I'd sooner work my uncle's farm for half the money than take a cheque for doing nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. Our church would help people who lost work, it always has. That's the help I'd trust most.

headlineQuote: I'd sooner work my uncle's farm for half the money than take a cheque for doing nothing.
portrait: Sam Larsen, 27, drives a **feed truck** for a farmers' co-op and is engaged to Ruth.
He's already uneasy about **farms selling up**, which shrinks his drops.
In the fast picture he expects to lose driving by 2031 and turns to his **uncle's farm**.
He prefers work and family over **handouts**, and admits he'd delay acting.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, newly married with no plan but family land.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** in farm machinery, honest early warning from the co-op, and church support.
